name: IVIG dose
seoDesc: IVIG dose: work out maternal blood volume from the weight and the fetal cells. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The IVIG dose calculator turns the weight, the fetal cells and the rhIG vials into maternal blood volume. Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the IVIG dose calculator work?
sections.html:
The IVIG dose calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports maternal blood volume in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the type of calculation and the sex); then you type in the weight (Hemolytic disease of the newborns), the fetal cells, the rhIG vials (300 µg in 30 mL) and the weight (General dosing).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as general and pregnancy hemorrhage. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “I know the maternal blood volume”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in kilograms. The unit chip switches it to any of the 29 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in percent. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • A number, expressed in #.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as female and male. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in kilograms. The unit chip switches it to any of the 29 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in grams. The unit chip switches it to any of the 29 supported units.

3 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the IVIG dose calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Maternal blood volume=30 × (rhIG vials (300 µg in 30 mL) − 1) ÷ fetal cells
Maternal blood volume=(3561 ÷ 10) × (height ^ 3) + (827 ÷ 25) × weight + 1833 ÷ 10
Ideal Body Weight=(11500 ÷ 127) × height − 88
Ideal Body Weight=(11500 ÷ 127) × height − 185 ÷ 2
BMI=weight ÷ (height ^ 2)
Ideal Body Weight=2 × dosing weight − weight

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Volume, opening in milliliters
  • %, opening in percent
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Mass, opening in kilograms

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The IVIG dose calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the weight, the fetal cells and the rhIG vials — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the IVIG dose calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns maternal blood volume, derived from the weight, the fetal cells and the rhIG vials. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the IVIG dose calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the weight, the fetal cells and the rhIG vials, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter weight (Hemolytic disease of the newborns) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Weight (Hemolytic disease of the newborns) opens in kilograms and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the IVIG dose calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
